steps.title: Fresh and herbal
steps.body: Verdejo gives crisp whites with lemon, grapefruit, green apple, fennel, bay leaf and fresh-cut grass, and a typical bitter almond finish. Acidity is medium to high, body light to medium. It's one of Spain's most popular whites, made mainly in Rueda, in Castilla y León.

steps.title: A revived grape
steps.body: Verdejo has grown in Rueda for centuries, probably brought from North Africa in the Middle Ages. It was long used for oxidised, Sherry-like wines. In 1972, the Rioja house Marqués de Riscal began making fresh, crisp Verdejo in Rueda, with cool fermentation. That modern style made Rueda famous; it became a DO in 1980.

steps.prompt: What changed Verdejo's style in the 1970s?
options: Marqués de Riscal's fresh, cool-fermented wines
steps.explanation: Riscal's modern approach created the fresh style Rueda is known for.

steps.title: Spotting it
steps.body: Look for pale lemon-green colour, citrus with herbal fennel and grassy notes, a crisp palate and a slightly bitter, almond finish. It's similar to Sauvignon Blanc, with which it's often blended, but more herbal, less pungent and with that bitter twist.

steps.prompt: Verdejo was once used for oxidised, Sherry-like wines.
steps.explanation: Yes. Before the 1970s, Rueda was known for oxidative styles.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Verdejo gives citrus, fennel and a bitter almond finish
It's grown in Rueda for centuries
Marqués de Riscal created its modern fresh style in 1972
